breakfast.name: Congee (Rice Porridge)
breakfast.description: Creamy rice porridge served with toppings like eggs, scallions, and pickled vegetables. Comfort food across China.
instructions: Rinse rice and add to large pot
Add broth and ginger slices
Bring to boil, then reduce heat to low
Simmer uncovered for 30-45 minutes, stirring occasionally
Rice should break down and create creamy porridge
Congee should be very soupy
Season with white pepper and salt
Pour into bowls
Top with century eggs, pork, peas, and scallions
Drizzle with sesame oil
Serve with pickled vegetables and crispy shallots
breakfast.notes: Congee can be made the night before and reheated. Adjust consistency with more broth if needed.
breakfast.fun_fact: Congee is eaten for breakfast, lunch, or dinner in China and is especially valued as a 'clean' food for when you're sick. The word 'congee' comes from Tamil.
alternatives: Vegetable toppings for vegetarian version
Different proteins (shrimp, beef)
Plain congee without toppings

lunch.name: Kung Pao Chicken
lunch.description: Spicy stir-fried chicken with peanuts, dried chilies, and vegetables. A classic Sichuan dish balancing heat, sweet, and savory.
instructions: Make sauce: Mix soy sauce, rice vinegar, sesame oil, sugar, and Sichuan peppercorn
Heat oil in wok or large skillet over high heat
Add chicken and cook until just cooked through, 5 minutes
Remove chicken and set aside
Add more oil if needed
Stir-fry dried chilies for 30 seconds until fragrant
Add garlic and ginger; cook 20 seconds
Add bell pepper and onion; cook 2-3 minutes until crisp-tender
Return chicken to wok
Add peanuts and sauce
Toss everything together for 1-2 minutes
Sauce should coat everything
Garnish with scallions
Serve immediately over rice
lunch.notes: The key is high heat and quick cooking. Everything should be prepared before you start cooking.
lunch.fun_fact: Kung Pao Chicken is named after Ding Baozhen, a Qing Dynasty official whose title was 'Kung Pao' (Palace Guardian). It originated in Sichuan province.
alternatives: Shrimp instead of chicken for seafood version
Cashews instead of peanuts
Reduce chilies for less spice

lunch.name: Peking Duck
lunch.description: A famous Beijing specialty - roasted duck with crispy skin served with thin pancakes, hoisin sauce, and cucumber. Requires special technique.
instructions: Clean duck thoroughly inside and outside
Blanch duck in boiling water for 1 minute to tighten skin
Mix honey, soy sauce, and rice vinegar in bowl
Brush this mixture all over duck skin
Let dry uncovered in refrigerator for 2 hours
Place star anise, ginger, garlic, and five-spice inside duck cavity
Hang duck or place on roasting rack in roasting pan
Add 2 cups water to pan
Roast at 400°F for 20 minutes
Reduce temperature to 325°F
Continue roasting for 60-90 minutes until skin is mahogany and crispy
Meat should be tender and juicy inside
Carve duck at table or in kitchen
Serve with thin pancakes, hoisin, cucumber, and scallions
Eat by spreading sauce on pancake, adding duck and vegetables, then rolling
lunch.notes: The key to crispy skin is low humidity and proper hanging. This is a Chinese restaurant specialty that's challenging at home.
lunch.fun_fact: Peking Duck has been a Beijing specialty since the Ming Dynasty. The most famous restaurant, Quanjude, has been serving it since 1864.
alternatives: Use regular oven instead of hanging
Roast chicken instead for easier option
Buy pre-roasted duck from Chinese market

dinner.name: Mapo Tofu
dinner.description: Silky tofu in a spicy, numbing Sichuan sauce with ground pork. Balance of heat, numbness, and savory flavors.
ingredients: 1 tbsp cornstarch mixed with 2 tbsp water
instructions: Heat oil in wok over medium-high heat
Cook ground pork, breaking apart, until done; set aside
Add more oil if needed
Add doubanjiang and fry for 1 minute until fragrant
Add garlic and ginger; cook 20 seconds
Add chili oil and Sichuan peppercorn powder
Pour in soy sauce, sugar, and broth
Bring to gentle simmer
Carefully add tofu cubes
Simmer for 5 minutes, gently stirring occasionally
Return pork to wok
Stir in cornstarch slurry
Cook until sauce thickens slightly and coats the tofu
Drizzle with sesame oil
Garnish with scallions
Serve immediately over rice
dinner.notes: Handle tofu gently to keep pieces intact. The numbing sensation from Sichuan peppercorn is characteristic and desired.
dinner.fun_fact: Mapo means 'pockmarked woman' - legend says it was invented by a pockmarked woman in Sichuan province. It's one of Sichuan's most iconic dishes.
alternatives: Beef instead of pork
Soft or firm tofu depending on preference
Reduce Sichuan peppercorn for less numbing

snacks.name: Dumplings (Jiaozi)
snacks.description: Filled dough pockets served steamed, boiled, or fried. A fundamental Chinese food and symbol of prosperity.
instructions: Make dough: Mix flour with boiling water
Add cold water gradually; knead until smooth
Cover and rest 30 minutes
Make filling: Mix pork with cabbage, scallions, ginger, garlic
Add soy sauce, sesame oil, sugar, salt, and pepper
Divide dough into 24 pieces; roll each into thin circle
Place 1 tbsp filling in center of each circle
Wet edges with water, fold into half-moon, then bring edges together
For steamed: Place in steamer basket on parchment, steam 8-10 minutes
For boiled: Drop in boiling water; simmer until they float plus 1 minute
For fried: Pan-fry until bottoms are crispy, then add water and cover to finish
Serve with dipping sauce (soy sauce, rice vinegar, sesame oil, chili oil)
snacks.notes: The wrapper-to-filling ratio is important - don't overstuff or they'll burst.
snacks.fun_fact: Dumplings are central to Chinese New Year celebrations, symbolizing prosperity and good luck. The shape resembles ancient Chinese gold ingots.
alternatives: Vegetarian filling with tofu and mushrooms
Shrimp and pork combination
Store-bought wrappers to save time

desserts.name: Mooncake
desserts.description: Traditional pastry with sweet filling, traditionally eaten during Mid-Autumn Festival. Dense, rich, and ornately decorated.
instructions: Make dough: Mix golden syrup with oil
Add flour and alkaline water
Knead until smooth; rest 30 minutes
Divide dough into 8 pieces, filling into 8 pieces
Flatten dough piece, add 1/4 cup lotus paste in center
If using egg yolk, wrap it in filling first
Bring dough edges together, seal
Roll into ball
Press into mooncake mold, pushing to compress
Press down firmly and turn out onto baking sheet
Brush with egg wash
Bake at 350°F for 15-20 minutes until golden
Cool on wire rack
Rest in airtight container for 2-3 days (skin will soften)
desserts.notes: Mooncakes improve with age - eat after 2-3 days when the filling has set properly.
desserts.fun_fact: Mooncakes are symbols of reunion and prosperity in Chinese culture. They're given as gifts and eaten during the Mid-Autumn Festival.
alternatives: Red bean paste instead of lotus paste
Salted egg yolk in the center
Store-bought mooncake molds for different designs

nonAlcoholicDrinks.name: Longjing Tea (Dragon Well Tea)
nonAlcoholicDrinks.description: Premium green tea from Hangzhou with delicate, chestnut flavor. One of China's most prized teas.
ingredients: 1 tsp Longjing tea leaves per cup
instructions: Heat water to 160-170°F (below boiling)
Warm teapot or cup by rinsing with hot water
Add Longjing leaves to infuser
Pour small amount of hot water over leaves
Let sit 30 seconds, then pour off (this is a rinse)
Pour fresh hot water over leaves
Steep for 2-3 minutes
Pour tea into serving cups
Can re-steep leaves several times
Drink while hot
nonAlcoholicDrinks.notes: Don't use boiling water - it will damage the delicate tea. Lower temperature brings out subtle flavors.
nonAlcoholicDrinks.fun_fact: Longjing tea is one of China's 'Top 10 Famous Teas.' It has been grown in the mountains near Hangzhou for over 1,200 years.
alternatives: Other green teas like Sencha or Matcha
Serve cold for summer version
Gongfu tea brewing method for more ceremonial preparation

alcoholicDrinks.name: Baijiu (Chinese Spirit)
alcoholicDrinks.description: Clear spirit distilled from sorghum or grains. The most consumed spirit in the world by volume. Served at celebrations.
instructions: This is an industrially produced spirit
Serve at room temperature in small glasses
Often drunk as a toast (bottom's up)
Pairs well with food
Strong and potent - drink respectfully
alcoholicDrinks.notes: Baijiu is complex - ranging from light and clean to strong and funky depending on production method.
alcoholicDrinks.fun_fact: Baijiu is the world's most-consumed spirit by volume. In Chinese culture, sharing baijiu represents friendship and business relationships.
alternatives: Shaoxing wine instead for more accessible option
Rice wine (huangjiu) for different style
Maotai for premium authentic brand
